457.history: A harbour on the eastern coast at the southern end of the shore A' Ghaoth Dhubh stripped. It fed the people of Cuan ruadh through the winter after the storm out of its shared surplus, and no one on that coast is known to have died of hunger that season. Rebuilding after A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the households set a stone in the midst of their houses and cut a plain stroke on it for every house the wind had taken, two-and-twenty marks in a row with no names beside them.
457.known_for: the stone of the twenty-two houses

119.history: The easternmost harbour of the island. In the two thousand four hundred and seventeenth year a storm out of the south-east stripped the thatch from every roof between Cuan ruadh and Ceann chiar and drove its boats onto the rocks below the headland; the coast named it A' Ghaoth Dhubh for the ash-dark sky it left behind. The valleys sent grain unasked, weighed by the count of mouths, and the coast called it only the bringing-in. The winter after, Lìleas, whose father's hand was maimed, kept a fire on the cape east of the village for boats coming home in the dark, the first of the five fires. Sixty years later the households laid stone to the eaves round the whole settlement, the first walls on that coast built against wind.
119.known_for: A' Ghaoth Dhubh, and Lìleas's fire

398.history: A southern cape where the households raised the last and surest of the five fires in the two thousand four hundred and twentieth year, on a mound of stacked stone breast-high, clear of the spray; a reciter of that coast named the five together before the mound was finished. The keepers of the fire built at last round a well whose water ran faintly red from the rock, and the settlement on the cape grew into the greatest place on the south coast, its fire burning nightly for boats that learned to watch for it.
398.known_for: the southern fire and the red well

433.history: A southern settlement near Imrich nam Pantar, where Gilleonan bored four holes along a hollow bird-bone in the two thousand four hundred and twenty-eighth year and found a note he could raise and lower at will; children of three households gathered to hear him play. The bone pipes are the oldest instruments of the island. The households kept watch on the passes in the crossing season, and in that same spring three great cats were seen to turn back at the highest pass.

257.history: A settlement a short walk inland of Baile ghorm, across whose fields the panthers' road ran. In the two thousand four hundred and thirty-first year its households began cutting a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scraping it away at its close, the first mark the island's tellers know cut for a season rather than for any one event; by the two thousand four hundred and forty-seventh year the custom was kept at every gate. The households shut their stock in while the cats passed.
257.known_for: the gatepost sign of the crossing season

475.history: A river-mouth settlement of fishing households on the north coast, at the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm. They fixed the custom of naming each boat for the wind it was built to fish in, held a boat unlucky under any other wind, and never gave a drowned boat's name again. The custom was settled by the two thousand four hundred and forty-seventh year and spread along the north coast with the wind-names themselves.

492.history: A small ford on the far eastern coast, settled in the four thousand three hundred and forty-seventh year, the easternmost dwelling of the age on the main island. Its households went out in boats after the geese on the islands offshore and raked salt from the flats beside the ford. It sent its geese-feathers inland by the traders' road and knew the hill only by report. The households kept the sharing before the storms as the coast kept it, weighing their surplus by the count of mouths on the shingle, and they cut the eight wind-names on a driftwood post above the landing so that a boat going out after the geese might know which wind would bring it home.

221.history: A smooth low island joined to the shore by a causeway on the eastern coast, where a few households settled in the three thousand one hundred and seventy-second year to live by the eggs and birds of the cliffs, trading feathers inland. A boy caught by dusk on a shelf below the highest nests was brought up by torchlight on a rope woven that same night, and from then no one of the settlement worked the cliffs alone: two to a rope, by custom rather than any law spoken. Its feathers went inland to the ford and to the valleys under Dùn ìseal, where they stuffed the bolsters of the king's kin in the waiting years.
221.known_for: the egg-cliffs and the two to a rope
